questions.stem: A reaction mixture warms from 19 °C to 21 °C as chemicals react. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is exothermic because heat was given out to the surroundings
options.explanation: A temperature rise means heat left the chemicals and warmed everything around them, which is the signature of an exothermic change.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic because the mixture absorbed heat
options.explanation: Endothermic changes take heat in and would cool the mixture; the reading rose instead of falling.

options.text: The reaction released no energy because the chemicals stayed liquid
options.explanation: Physical state does not decide heat flow; the measured temperature rise does.

options.text: The thermometer manufactured the extra heat
options.explanation: The thermometer records the temperature; the reaction supplies the heat it reports.

questions.stem: Which set of reaction types always gives energy out?

options.text: Neutralisation and combustion
options.explanation: Both reaction types always release heat to the surroundings.

options.text: Displacement and combustion
options.explanation: Displacement reactions can take energy in or give it out, so they do not always release heat.

options.text: Displacement and neutralisation
options.explanation: Neutralisation does release heat, but displacement can run in either energy direction.

options.text: Endothermic and combustion
options.explanation: Endothermic reactions take heat in, so the pairing cannot be correct.

questions.stem: Why does the temperature of the surroundings rise during an exothermic reaction?

options.text: Heat released by the reaction flows into the surroundings
options.explanation: Energy given out by the chemicals has nowhere to go except the surroundings, warming them.

options.text: The surroundings supply the energy for the reaction
options.explanation: That describes an endothermic change; exothermic reactions hand energy over instead.

options.text: The reaction destroys energy so none remains in the chemicals
options.explanation: Energy is conserved; it is transferred, never destroyed.

options.text: The products store the released heat permanently
options.explanation: The heat passes to the surroundings; the products end with less energy than the reactants.

questions.stem: In an endothermic reaction, what happens to the energy of the system?

options.text: It increases because heat is taken in from the surroundings
options.explanation: Energy absorbed from the surroundings raises the heat content of the system.

options.text: It decreases because energy leaves the system
options.explanation: An endothermic change pulls energy in; a falling energy content describes exothermic reactions.

options.text: It stays exactly the same throughout the change
options.explanation: Total energy is conserved, but the share held by the system changes when heat crosses the boundary.

options.text: It becomes impossible to measure with school apparatus
options.explanation: A thermometer in the mixture tracks the change directly.

questions.stem: The products of a reaction have less energy than the reactants. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The reaction was exothermic and heat was transferred to the surroundings
options.explanation: A lower product energy means energy left the chemicals as heat.

options.text: The reaction was endothermic and heat entered the chemicals
options.explanation: Heat entering would leave the products with more energy, not less.

options.text: Energy was created inside the reaction mixture
options.explanation: Energy is never created; the drop matches the heat handed over to the surroundings.

options.text: No energy conclusion can be drawn from energy levels
options.explanation: The energy difference is exactly the evidence needed to classify the reaction.

questions.stem: State the temperature change observed in the reaction mixture during an exothermic reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Exothermic reactions give heat energy out to the surroundings, so the temperature of the reaction mixture rises.

questions.stem: State the direction of temperature movement inside an endothermic reaction mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: Endothermic reactions take heat in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the reaction mixture falls.

questions.stem: Explain why a displacement reaction cannot be classified from its type alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Displacement reactions can transfer energy either way, so some give heat out while others take it in, and only the measured temperature change reveals which.

questions.stem: Two unknown reactions are set up side by side, each with a thermometer in the mixture. State what single reading separates exothermic from endothermic in each tube.
questions.modelAnswer: Whether the thermometer shows a rise or a fall separates them: a temperature rise marks an exothermic change and a fall marks an endothermic one.

questions.stem: A student claims energy was destroyed in a reaction that cooled. What is the correct response?

options.text: Energy was transferred to the surroundings, not destroyed
options.explanation: The law of conservation of energy forbids destruction; the heat simply moved out of the mixture.

options.text: Energy was destroyed because the temperature fell
options.explanation: A falling temperature signals heat leaving, not energy vanishing.

options.text: Energy was created inside the thermometer bulb
options.explanation: The thermometer only reports temperature; it does not manufacture energy.

options.text: The law of conservation of energy does not apply to chemical reactions
options.explanation: The law applies to every reaction; energy changes location but persists.

questions.stem: Why do the products of an exothermic reaction hold less energy than the reactants?

options.text: The missing energy was released to the surroundings as heat
options.explanation: Conservation requires the energy difference to appear somewhere, and it leaves as heat.

options.text: The products are always colder, so they store less
options.explanation: Temperature is a reading, not the energy ledger; the difference is the transferred heat.

options.text: Some energy was destroyed while bonds rearranged
options.explanation: No energy disappears; it is transferred to the surroundings.

options.text: The products gained energy from the surroundings
options.explanation: Gaining energy would make the products richer in energy, the opposite of the observation.

questions.stem: Which pairing of reaction type and energy direction is correct?

options.text: Combustion gives energy out; displacement may give energy out or take it in
options.explanation: Combustion always releases heat, while displacement appears in both directions in the list of heat changes.

options.text: Combustion takes energy in; neutralisation gives it out
options.explanation: Combustion always gives energy out; only the second half of the pairing is right.

options.text: Neutralisation takes energy in; combustion takes it in
options.explanation: Both named types give energy out.

options.text: Displacement always takes energy in; combustion gives it out
options.explanation: Displacement can run either way, so the word always makes the claim wrong.

questions.stem: A table shows four experiments; one mixture cools while three warm. What classifies the cooling one?

options.text: Endothermic, because its temperature fell as heat was taken in
options.explanation: A temperature drop marks heat flowing from the surroundings into the mixture.

options.text: Exothermic, because most reactions are exothermic
options.explanation: Classification follows the measured direction, not the frequency of reaction types.

options.text: Impossible to classify without a balanced equation
options.explanation: The temperature change alone classifies the reaction.

options.text: Endothermic, because one chemical in it is a weak acid
options.explanation: The classification rests on the observed temperature fall, not on the identity of a single chemical.

questions.stem: Where does the energy transferred in a reaction end up if the mixture warms?

options.text: In the surroundings, including the thermometer and the air around the cup
options.explanation: The heat spreads to everything touching the mixture, which is what the thermometer detects.

options.text: Nowhere, because the reaction consumed it
options.explanation: Energy is conserved; the warming shows it moved to the surroundings.

options.text: In the reactants, which store extra energy afterwards
options.explanation: The reactants are spent; the products hold less energy than they did.

options.text: Only in the products, which stay hot forever
options.explanation: The products share their energy with the surroundings as the mixture cools.

questions.stem: State the law that says energy cannot be created or destroyed.
questions.modelAnswer: The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.

questions.stem: State two reaction types that always give energy out.
questions.modelAnswer: Neutralisation and combustion are exothermic examples that always give energy out.

questions.stem: Account for the energy gap that opens between products and reactants in an exothermic change.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy released moved to the surroundings, and because energy is conserved the products must hold less energy than the reactants by exactly the amount transferred.

questions.stem: A results table lists temperature changes of -6, +2 and -9 degrees Celsius for three reactions. State how the table classifies each row.
questions.modelAnswer: The negative temperature changes mark endothermic rows and the positive change marks an exothermic row, so the table classifies each reaction by the sign of its temperature change.
